newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Ecus rally but EMU doubts still lurk.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Ecus rally but EMU doubts still lurk.

text.p: Ecu bonds have rallied strongly this year on a wave of optimism over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) but doubts will continue to plague the illiquid market until EMU actually happens, analysts said.
The Ecu will continue to narrow the spread on German Bunds but the slightest question over the 1999 start date could send that gap swinging sharply out, they said on Wednesday.
"As long as people are optimistic that EMU is going to take place they should be buying the Ecu market," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Europe.
The 10-year Ecu/Bund yield spread has narrowed to around 38 basis points from around 90 at the beginning of the year and analysts said it should continue to march in.
A risk premium on Ecus remained however, analysts said.

"Until monetary union takes place there always ought to be some sort of risk factor in there in case it is delayed so I wouldn't expect the spread to disappear until it (EMU) actually happens," Jessop said.

He said Ecu bonds were doubly vulnerable to such concerns, firstly because the basket of markets which make up the Ecu would weaken if EMU were delayed, and secondly because the Ecu is trading at a premium to the theoretical Ecu.
The actual Ecu is currently trading around 10 basis points lower than the theoretical Ecu basket, Jessop said.
"The risk is not only that the yield on the basket rises, but that the Ecu itself underperforms the basket as well. So you've got a double whammy on the Ecu market," Jessop said.

Paul Eustace, head of Ecu bond trading at BZW said much of the positive sentiment about EMU was already priced into the market but this would not deter investors from continuing to buy Ecu bonds if they firmly believed EMU would take place on time.
However, should any of the senior European politicians promoting EMU start to express doubts over the process, there would be a sharp negative reaction, he said.

"If sentiment turns nasty on monetary union, as a trader in the market you really have nowhere to go with the bond," he said. "It is not a market in its own right, it is a market driven solely by sentiment and you tend to find all the clients want to do the same thing at the same time. That is why liquidity is so poor."
Eustace said unlike other bond markets, Ecu bonds had no backstop investors who would be prepared to step in when the market was cheap.
An analyst at a French bank in Paris said there was nothing to stop the convergence of Ecu bonds towards OATs and Bunds over the next two years.
"The only thing that would push Ecu spreads wider would be if EMU was not to happen, but people don't believe that will be the case," she said.

"The spreads are a little wide at the moment because people are worrying about the criteria of the stability pact but in two years time Ecus should be flat to OATs and Bunds," the French analyst said, adding that the problem was rather over who would take part at the start of EMU.

She said if Italy could re-enter the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) by the end of the year and thereby be able to fulfill the Maastricht criteria of a minimum two year membership of the ERM, there was a good chance it would join EMU in 1999.
But regardless of Italy, or Spain, being in at the start, EMU would begin on time, she said.
"It is better to see a hard Ecu in 1999 than to wait one or two years for some more countries," she said.
She said on the premise that EMU did go ahead in 1999 many French investors were buying the 2005 Ecu.
"It has the same coupon and coupon date as the 2005 French franc OAT so they will be truly fungible in 1999."
